scan.summary: This is Cascade Specialty Chemicals' internal policy describing how the Portland facility's 42 employees must respond to fires, chemical releases, medical emergencies, earthquakes, and other emergencies. The plan covers alarm signals, evacuation routes and assembly procedures, employee accounting, medical response, and staff training requirements. It is not a permit or certificate issued by an agency, but rather an internal operational policy required under workplace safety regulations.
scan.freshness_note: The document was last revised in February 2021, nearly five years old. The plan specifies annual review by the facilities lead every January (Section 6), so a new version may be overdue. Ask whether the January 2026 review was completed and whether the plan has been updated since.

gaps.title: Missing last review or update date
gaps.description: The document states the facilities lead reviews the plan every January, but does not record when that review was last done or whether the plan was updated after the February 2021 revision.
gaps.fix: Add a line stating the date of the most recent annual review and any updates made. For example: 'Last reviewed and updated: January 2026.'
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) requires emergency action plans be reviewed and updated at least annually.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.

gaps.title: Missing rescue and medical response training documentation
gaps.description: The plan names two first-aid responders per shift and states they are trained, but does not specify what training they have received (e.g., CPR, First Aid certification level, dates of most recent training).
gaps.fix: Maintain records showing the name, certification type, certification number, and expiry date for each first-aid responder. Document that floor wardens receive annual training and keep records of training dates and topics.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) requires employers to ensure that all designated personnel are trained. Oregon also requires first-aid and CPR training records.
gaps.locator: Section 5, Rescue and medical duties, and Section 6, Training and review
gaps.quote: First aid is given at the assembly point by the trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster)

gaps.title: Missing fire alarm system maintenance and test records
gaps.description: The plan states the alarm is tested on the first Monday of each month but does not require records of those tests. It does not require documentation that Cascade Fire & Safety's 24-hour monitoring and maintenance is current.
gaps.fix: Maintain a log showing the date and result of each monthly alarm test. Maintain records showing the service contract with Cascade Fire & Safety, its renewal date, and copies of their quarterly or annual maintenance reports.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) and NFPA 72 (National Fire Alarm Code) require fire alarm systems to be tested and serviced regularly with records kept.
gaps.quote: The alarm is tested on the first Monday of each month by the facilities lead.

gaps.title: Missing drill documentation and records
gaps.description: The plan states evacuation drills are held twice a year (spring and autumn) but does not require records of dates, number of participants, problems found, or corrective actions taken.
gaps.fix: Maintain a log of each evacuation drill showing the date, time, participants, duration, any problems encountered, and corrective actions taken. Document that drills are completed and reviewed.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) requires emergency action plans include procedures for practices and drills and that records be kept.
gaps.locator: Section 4, Accounting for employees after evacuation
gaps.quote: Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.

gaps.title: Missing incident coordinator designation and training
gaps.description: Section 4 references an 'incident coordinator at the assembly point' who communicates with the fire department, but the plan does not name who this person is or confirm they have been trained for this role.
gaps.fix: Designate one or more incident coordinators by name and title. Specify their training and confirm they understand the role. Note backup designations in case the primary is unavailable.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) requires designation of personnel responsible for emergency response roles.
gaps.locator: Section 4, Accounting for employees after evacuation
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire department on arrival.

gaps.title: Missing emergency contact and notification procedures
gaps.description: The plan does not describe how management or emergency responders will be notified in an actual emergency, or how employees will be informed of an all-clear or updated information during an incident.
gaps.fix: Add a section on emergency notification, including phone numbers for key personnel to be called, who is responsible for notifying off-site staff or family members, and how updates will be communicated (e.g., text, email, phone tree).
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) requires procedures for notifying emergency responders and affected persons.

gaps.title: Missing critical infrastructure shutdown and utility procedures
gaps.description: The plan mentions the facilities lead shutting down ventilation in a shelter-in-place event (Section 3) but does not describe procedures for stopping chemical operations, closing gas or water valves, or other steps to contain a hazard.
gaps.fix: Add a section describing what equipment or processes must be shut down in different emergency scenarios (fire, chemical release, medical emergency). Specify who is trained to perform these shutdowns and where control panels or valves are located.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) requires procedures for shutdown of operations at the facility.
gaps.locator: Section 3, Evacuation procedures; Section 5, Rescue and medical duties
gaps.quote: the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel

gaps.title: Missing communication with individuals with special needs
gaps.description: The plan does not address how employees with mobility limitations, hearing or visual impairments, or other conditions that affect emergency response will be accommodated during evacuation or shelter-in-place.
gaps.fix: Add a section on accommodations for employees with disabilities or special needs. Note that floor wardens should be aware of employees requiring assistance and that assembly point procedures should account for mobility-limited individuals.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a)(5) requires the emergency action plan address rescue and medical duties and specifically require consideration of persons unable to exit the facility unassisted.
gaps.locator: Section 3, Evacuation procedures; Section 5, Rescue and medical duties

expected_missing.title: Injury and incident reporting procedures
expected_missing.why: A company this size with chemical operations should have a written procedure for documenting and reporting workplace injuries, chemical exposures, and near-misses.

expected_missing.title: Chemical inventory and hazard summary
expected_missing.why: An emergency action plan for a chemical manufacturer should reference or be accompanied by a summary of hazardous chemicals on site, including quantities and storage locations, to help responders understand the threat.

expected_missing.title: Medical emergency procedures specific to chemical exposure
expected_missing.why: Beyond directing exposure victims to the emergency shower, the plan should name specific first-aid treatments for the chemicals in use (e.g., for ingestion, inhalation, skin contact).

expected_missing.title: Restoration and business continuity procedures
expected_missing.why: The plan should address how to resume operations safely after an emergency and communicate with customers or suppliers of delays.

expected_missing.title: Post-emergency debriefing and documentation
expected_missing.why: A procedure for documenting lessons learned, near-misses, or actual events to improve future preparedness.

scan.confidence_notes: This plan was read completely and is clearly written. I am confident in the facts stated and the gaps identified regarding missing documentation, records, and supporting procedures. The plan itself meets the basic structure required by OSHA 1910.38(a) — it covers evacuation, accounting for employees, rescue and medical duties, and training. However, the significant gaps are in supporting documentation: no record dates are shown for reviews, drills, training, or alarm tests, and no supporting records are mentioned as being maintained. At nearly five years since the last revision, it is overdue for the annual January review specified in Section 6. I am not able to confirm from this document alone whether those supporting records exist in the company's files. A medium-to-high confidence rating is appropriate: the plan itself is sound, but its effectiveness depends on records and annual updates that are not evident from the document provided.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
